name: Deal with human waste
summary: First find out whether the drains still work. On a septic system that runs by gravity, a bucket of non-drinking water poured fast into the bowl still flushes it. In town, assume the sewage lift stations stop with the power: flush solids only and pour nothing else down the drains. If sewage backs up, a septic pump or other electrical part has no power, or the pipes are frozen, stop flushing and use a bucket toilet: two bags in a lidded pail, with sawdust, ash or cat litter. For a long outage outside town, a pit latrine or compost toilet takes over, well away from wells, lakes and streams; King County says latrines don't suit urban areas. Frozen ground is hard to dig, doesn't drain and can slump when it thaws, so plan before freeze-up. Gloves for emptying and cleaning, and soap and water beside every toilet.

parts.why: Lidded pails for bucket toilets and buckets of flush water
Tying off bags, emptying pails and cleaning
Heavy liners, and covers over a pit or compost pile
Seat, floor and shelter for a latrine or compost toilet
Vent pipe for a ventilated pit latrine
Privacy screen and a rain cover
Splash protection when emptying or cleaning up sewage

tips: Bucket flush: pour about 4.5 L (1.2 US gal) quickly into the bowl from 30 to 60 cm (1 to 2 ft) up, so the rush starts the siphon (ACWD). Use non-drinking water (Alberta water shortages), not stored wash water, which turns septic (WHO EMRO).

A bucket flush only works where the drains run: a gravity septic tank and field keeps working without power (Texas A&M AgriLife). With a septic pump or other electrical parts stopped, Texas A&M says to stop all water use in a long outage: use a bucket toilet.

In town, lift stations stop with the power: West Hants asks for solids-only flushing and no liquids poured down drains, kept up for about an hour after the power returns (West Hants). The sewer backup guide covers what to do when sewage comes up.

If sewage comes up a drain, stay out of the water, switch the power off only from a dry spot, and run pumps and generators outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents (CDC flooded home).

Bucket toilet: two heavy bags in a 19 L (5 US gal) pail or the toilet bowl, with cat litter, ash or sawdust in the bottom and a shut lid. Tie the bags off daily and keep them somewhere protected, such as a garage, until a safe way to get rid of them opens up (King County).

Keep pits and compost toilets at least 30 m from water and the pit bottom 1.5 m above the water table, if you can't test the soil (Sphere). Ontario's legal minimum for privies and composting toilets is 15 m from a drilled well, lake or stream and 30 m from a dug well (TBDHU). Use the larger figures.

A pit dug in frozen ground can cave in when it thaws: rest the slab on planks or poles reaching 1 m past each side (WEDC Guide 29). Don't stand in a pit deeper than 1.2 m (4 ft) unless its sides are sloped or shored, and keep a second person at the top (CCOHS trenching).
Seal a VIP latrine's vent pipe as the cold sets in: in very cold months it pulls the pit's warmth away. Below freezing, waste stops breaking down and pits fill faster (WEDC Guide 29).

Wash hands with soap after every visit, from a tippy tap or a jug beside the toilet (Sphere). Sphere lists ash as an alternative to soap, but a Cochrane review couldn't tell whether ash works as well as soap (Cochrane ash review).
Never climb into a septic tank: its gases can kill, and they burn, so keep flames and sparks away and the lid secure (FVRD). Treat a pump chamber or a deep pit the same way.
